opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is that deployment gives you a kind of signal you just can't get from any static benchmark. When we build evals internally, we're always constrained by our own imagination. We pick the tasks, we write the prompts, we decide what "good" looks like. And benchmarks saturate quickly; once a number gets close to the ceiling, it stops telling you much about what the model can actually do for people.

When you put a model in front of a huge, diverse set of users, they find things you never would have thought to test. People bring their real workflows: messy codebases, strange domain-specific questions, long multi-step tasks. That surfaces both capabilities and failure modes you didn't know were there. Some of the most interesting behaviors we've learned about came from users pushing the model in directions nobody on the team anticipated.

There's also a grounding effect. It's easy to get excited about a few points on some academic eval, but the real question is whether the model is more useful. Do people come back? Do they trust it with harder problems? Does it save them time? Deployment keeps you honest about that.

And on the safety side, iterative deployment matters a lot. You learn how models get misused, where the guardrails are too tight or too loose, and you get to fix those things while the stakes are relatively lower, rather than discovering them all at once with a much more capable system. So for me, broad deployment isn't a replacement for careful internal evaluation. It's the complement that closes the loop between what we think the model can do and what it actually does in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says users bring real workflows, including messy codebases, and that these reveal unexpected failure modes. That clearly covers discovering software-task failures.

r002.rationale: It says deployment surfaces capabilities, but does not state what range or level of math or software work models can handle.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that our internal evals, no matter how good they get, are always a proxy. They're a snapshot of what we thought to ask. And the moment you put a model in front of millions of people, you discover the distribution of things people actually want to do is way wider and way weirder than anything we wrote down ahead of time.

There are a couple of specific things I find valuable about it. The first is just coverage. People use these models for things we never anticipated, and a lot of the most interesting failure modes don't show up on a benchmark. They show up when someone in a completely different domain pushes on the model in a way nobody on the team would have thought to. Broad deployment is basically the largest, most diverse red team you can get, and it's also the largest, most diverse set of people telling you what's actually useful.

The second is that it keeps us honest about what matters. It's really easy inside a lab to get obsessed with moving a number on a leaderboard, and sometimes that number doesn't correlate with whether anyone's life got better. When you ship, you find out pretty quickly whether the capability you were proud of actually lands. Sometimes something we considered a minor improvement turns out to matter enormously to users, and sometimes the thing we spent months on just doesn't move the needle for anyone.

And the third piece, which I think is underrated, is that it's the only real way to learn about safety at scale. You can do all the adversarial testing you want internally, but the world is more creative than your red team. Seeing how the model behaves in the wild, where it's being used by people with different intentions and different levels of sophistication, gives you signal you just can't manufacture in a lab. And you get to iterate. You ship, you observe, you fix, you ship again. That loop is where a lot of the real progress comes from.

The caveat, obviously, is that you have to be thoughtful about it. You don't just dump the most capable thing you have on the world and see what happens. It's gradual, it's measured, and you want to have the monitoring in place so that when you learn something, you actually learn it rather than finding out six months later. But done carefully, I think it's one of the most informative evaluation methods we have.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest value is that people use models in ways you wouldn’t anticipate. When you evaluate internally, you’re choosing the tasks, so you’re also bringing your assumptions about what matters. Broad deployment lets you see where those assumptions break down—what people actually want to do, where the model is useful, and where it falls short.

That feedback can reveal gaps that a benchmark doesn’t capture. A model might get a question right but still be frustrating to work with because it misunderstands the intent or needs too much guidance. Deployment helps you understand that difference. It complements controlled evaluations and gives you a much richer picture of what to improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is that people use these models in ways we wouldn’t have anticipated. Internally, we can build evaluations for the capabilities we care about, but that’s still a pretty narrow view of what people actually want to do. Broad deployment gives you feedback from a much wider range of tasks and contexts.

And you discover that a model can look great on a benchmark but still be frustrating to use. Maybe it misunderstands what someone wants, or it takes too much back-and-forth to get a useful answer. Seeing those interactions helps us understand what we’re missing in our evaluations and what we should work on next.
